Natterer's bat (Myotis nattereri) exhibits a life-history strategy shaped by the energetic constraints of hibernation and temperate-zone insectivory. Under the thermal conditions typical of the active season (approximately 34.8 °C [T = 34.8 °C]), gestation lasts 54 days [tg = 54 days], a thermoregulatory investment that supports rapid foetal development. The neonatal pups are remarkably small, with a wet weight at birth of just 0.79 grams [Wwb = 0.79 grams], a mass that underscores the altricial state typical of vespertilionid newborns. This modest birth mass imposes a substantial dependency period; the young rely entirely on maternal milk for nourishment. Field records indicate that weaning, marking the nutritional independence of the offspring, occurs at 60 days since birth [tx = 60 days since birth] under the same sustained thermal regime at a temperature of 34.8 °C [T = 34.8 °C]. The extended lactation interval reflects the slow pace of somatic development in this species, likely an adaptation to the unpredictable availability of aerial insect prey.

Reproductive output in Myotis nattereri is constrained by the brevity of the temperate summer and the high energetic cost of lactation. Females give birth to a single pup per litter [N_R_i = single pup per litter], and, critically, produce only one litter each year [F_R_i = one litter each year]. This low fecundity is typical of the genus, reflecting a strategy that prioritizes offspring quality over quantity in an environment where foraging success is highly variable. The entire reproductive cycle, from parturition through weaning, is timed to coincide with peak insect abundance in mid-summer. The pup, dependent on maternal milk and body heat, grows gradually in the relative safety of the maternity roost before attaining sufficient size and flight ability to forage independently. The prolonged association between mother and offspring facilitates the transfer of foraging skills and knowledge of roost locations, which are critical for juvenile survival during the first autumn.

Puberty in Natterer's bat is not achieved until well after the first winter of life. Available data indicate that the time since birth at puberty is 365 days [tp = 365 days], a remarkably long interval for a mammal of this body size, and this milestone is reached under the typical euthermic body temperature of 34.8 °C [T = 34.8 °C] during the active season. This extended period of juvenile development contrasts sharply with the rapid maturation seen in many small rodent species. The delay in pubertal onset is thought to reflect the time required for young bats to accumulate sufficient fat reserves for hibernation and to attain the skeletal and flight-muscle maturity necessary for successful foraging and predator avoidance. As a result, first reproduction is typically deferred until the summer following their second year of life, a life-history pattern that contributes to the species' relatively slow population turnover rate.

The maximum longevity of Natterer's bat is notable for an animal of its size. Long-term banding studies have documented individuals surviving for 23.7 years [am = 23.7 years], a lifespan that rivals or exceeds that of many larger mammals at a temperature of 34.8 °C [T = 34.8 °C]. This extreme longevity, which occurs under the same approximate body temperature of 34.8 °C [T = 34.8 °C] during active periods, is a hallmark of the slow life-history strategy common among hibernating bats. The combination of a low annual reproductive output, a late age at first breeding, and an extraordinarily long lifespan places Myotis nattereri at the slow end of the mammalian life-history continuum. This strategy is thought to be an evolutionary response to high adult survival rates, which are favored in environments where juvenile mortality from predation or stochastic weather events is high, and where the ability to survive multiple hibernation cycles confers a strong selective advantage.

Basal metabolic rate in Myotis nattereri reflects the energetic economy required to sustain its life-history strategy. Respirometry trials conducted on resting, post-absorptive individuals at a body temperature of 34.8 °C [T = 34.8 °C] measured a maximum basal oxygen consumption of 8.70 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 8.70 milliliters of oxygen per hour]. This value is consistent with the low mass-specific metabolic rates reported for other insectivorous bats in the genus Myotis. The modest metabolic expenditure is offset by the species' ability to enter daily torpor during inclement weather, thereby conserving energy when foraging is impossible. Furthermore, the ultimate wet weight for adult females, which averages 9.5 grams [Wwi = 9.5 grams], represents the upper range of body mass reported for the species, with individuals typically ranging from 5 to 9.5 grams depending on reproductive status, season, and prey availability. This relatively stable adult mass, combined with a low metabolic rate and a long lifespan, exemplifies a bet-hedging strategy that buffers the population against the pronounced interannual variability in insect abundance characteristic of northern temperate regions.
